title: Ninth commandment (CCC 2517–2533)
hook: purity of heart lets us see God in others

segments.voice: Yesterday, truth and beauty: real beauty can tell the truth. Your line was beauty is true. What stopped you, even for a moment? A new week. Day one thousand one hundred thirty-five.

A smudge on a pair of glasses. The wearer doesn't notice it at first. The world just seems to have gone a little gray, a little blurred at the edges, and faces look tired. Then the glasses come off, get a wipe on a shirt, go back on, and everything is sharp again. Nothing out there changed. The lens did. The ninth commandment, in the Catechism, turns out to be about lenses: what we look at people through. Today's word is the clean one.
screen: `A SMUDGE ON YOUR GLASSES.` → `NOTHING OUT THERE CHANGED.` → `THE LENS DID.`

segments.voice: The ninth commandment, as the Catechism counts them, forbids coveting a neighbor's wife: disordered desire, which the Catechism calls concupiscence. But the Catechism builds the whole section on a line from the Sermon on the Mount. In the Douay-Rheims: "Blessed are the clean of heart: for they shall see God." The heart, here, isn't just feelings. The Catechism calls it the seat of the moral personality: in plain words, where intentions are born. And it says the pure of heart are those who have tuned their mind and will to God's ways, in charity, in chastity, in love of truth, and in faith. Then comes the promise, and the Catechism opens it in a surprising direction. Seeing God is the end of the road. But purity of heart starts letting us see according to God now. It lets us take in the other person as a neighbor. It lets us see the human body, our own and others', as a temple of the Holy Spirit. That's the smudge wiped off. Not a refusal to look at people, but a way of looking that doesn't reduce them. How does a heart get clean? The Catechism is practical. It names a struggle, and the helps for it: chastity, purity of intention, purity of vision, discipline over what we let our feelings and imagination dwell on, and prayer. It adds modesty, which it describes as protecting the private center of a person, and refusing to unveil what should stay hidden. And it's honest that this is grace as well as effort: no one cleans the lens entirely alone. So the ninth commandment isn't mainly a list of things not to see. It's a promise about what you'll be able to see.
screen: `BLESSED ARE THE CLEAN OF HEART.` · `THE HEART: WHERE INTENTIONS ARE BORN.` · `SEE OTHERS AS GOD SEES THEM.` · `CHASTITY, INTENTION, VISION, PRAYER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look at people with clean eyes. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind three faces: someone you love, someone you pass every day without really seeing, and someone you find hard. One at a time, let each face come into focus. Set down the label you usually stick on them. Look for the person underneath. If you pray, you can ask to see each one as God sees them. If you don't, just look, and let them be more than you thought. The bell holds the time.
Purity of heart. A heart tuned to God in love, chastity, truth and faith, which, in Catholic teaching, begins to see others, and God, clearly. Today's word.
Your line: they shall see god. Today, when you catch yourself sizing someone up, wipe the lens, and look again. Day one thousand one hundred thirty-five.

howItsDone: Catholics pray for purity of heart and examine their thoughts and looks before confession; the Church teaches chastity, modesty, purity of intention and prayer as helps in this struggle.

fork.setup: the beatitude promises the clean of heart that they shall see God. when does the Catechism say that seeing begins?
options: already now, in how we see others.
fork.reveal: seeing God is the goal, but the Catechism says purity of heart already lets us see according to God: the other as a neighbor, the body as a temple.

notes: CCC paraphrased throughout (copyrighted translation). Check: heart as seat of the moral personality (2517); the pure of heart attuned in charity, chastity, love of truth and orthodoxy of faith (2518); seeing 'according to God', the body as temple (2519); the four helps (2520); modesty protecting the intimate center of the person (2521).
Index title cites CCC 2517–2533; the section opens at 2514 (Exodus 20:17 and Matthew 5:28). 'As the Catechism counts them' acknowledges the Catholic numbering of the commandments.
'Faith' stands in for CCC 2518's 'orthodoxy of faith'; confirm.
Editor: hook recast in the third person so it no longer tells the listener what they think or notice.

Editor (second pass): 'four helps' count removed (CCC 2520 lists more than four: chastity, purity of intention, purity of vision, discipline of feelings and imagination, refusing complicity in impure thoughts, prayer); 'desire that treats a person as something to take' replaced with CCC 2514's own word, concupiscence; 'where intentions are born' marked as the lesson's gloss.

Audit (1132–1141 pass): no changes. Matthew 5:8 (Douay-Rheims), Greek καθαροὶ τῇ καρδίᾳ, and CCC 2514–2521 (seat of moral personality, seeing 'according to God', body as temple, the helps, modesty) checked and found accurate. The practice (seeing people whole) sits near day 1130's; the lens image and three-faces structure keep it distinct.
